lesson.title: o→ue & e→ie: puedo, duermo, empiezo
lesson.subtitle: Why the vowel splits inside the singular and 3rd-person plural boot, and stays single in nosotros

hook.title: Mastering the Two Diphthong Boots: o→ue and e→ie
hook.content:
Let's put our two biggest boot-verb families side by side:
• **o → ue under stress**: **poder** ('to be able to / can' → puedo, puedes, puede, *podemos*, pueden), **dormir** ('to sleep' → duermo, duermes, duerme, *dormimos*, duermen), **mostrar** ('to show' → muestro, muestras, muestra, *mostramos*, muestran), **recordar** ('to remember' → recuerdo, *recordamos*).
• **e → ie under stress**: **querer** (quiero, *queremos*), **tener** (tienes, *tenemos*), **empezar** ('to begin' → empiezo, empiezas, empieza, *empezamos*, empiezan), **preferir** ('to prefer' → prefiero, prefieres, prefiere, *preferimos*, prefieren)!

pattern.title: The Nosotros Anchor
pattern.content: Whenever you say 'we' (nosotros), the stress lands on **-amos / -emos / -imos**, so the stem vowel NEVER splits: podemos, dormimos, mostramos, queremos, tenemos, empezamos, preferimos!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: puedo / podemos, duermo / dormimos, muestro / mostramos, empiezo / empezamos, prefiero / preferimos
exercises.meaning: I can / we can (poder: o→ue), I sleep / we sleep (dormir: o→ue), I show / we show (mostrar: o→ue), I start / we start (empezar: e→ie), I prefer / we prefer (preferir: e→ie)
exercises.explanation: Inside the boot = split vowel (ue / ie); outside the boot (nosotros) = single vowel (o / e).

exercises.prompt: Build 'I prefer' from 'preferir' by splitting the second 'e' into 'ie' and adding '-o':
exercises.explanation: preferir splits the stressed e (the one right before -ir) into ie: prefiero!

exercises.prompt: Compare 'I prefer coffee' and 'We prefer coffee'. Which pair is 100% accurate?
options: Yo prefiero el café / Nosotros preferimos el café
Yo prefero el café / Nosotros prefieremos el café
Yo prefiero el café / Nosotros prefierimos el café
exercises.target_answer: Yo prefiero el café / Nosotros preferimos el café
exercises.meaning: I prefer coffee / We prefer coffee
exercises.explanation: Stressed stem in yo prefiero splits e→ie; unstressed stem in nosotros preferimos stays single e!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I prefer the coffee, but we can drink water'
exercises.target_answer: Prefiero el café, pero podemos beber agua
exercises.meaning: I prefer the coffee, but we can drink water
exercises.explanation: Prefiero (stressed stem → ie) + pero podemos (unstressed stem → o).

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Duermo ocho horas por la noche
exercises.target_answer: Duermo ocho horas por la noche
exercises.meaning: I sleep eight hours at night
exercises.explanation: Duermo ocho horas por la noche.

summary.outcome: Switch effortlessly between stressed boot forms (puedo, duermo, empiezo, prefiero) and unstressed nosotros forms (podemos, dormimos, empezamos, preferimos).

use_example.german: Prefiero el café por la mañana y duermo ocho horas por la noche.
use_example.english: I prefer coffee in the morning and I sleep eight hours at night.

summary.takeaway: Follow your voice stress: stressed stem splits (ie/ue); stressed ending (-amos/-emos/-imos) stays single.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([5112] e→i & -go Verbs: pido, digo, hago, pongo): master the e→i boot and the famous -go squad!

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'Can you show me the house?'

poder.english_meaning: to be able to, can (puedo: I can)
poder.shift_rule: Boot verb o → ue (puedo, puedes, puede, podemos)
poder.etymology_derivation: Vulgar Latin *potēre — root of potent and potential.

puedo.english_meaning: I can, I am able to
puedo.etymology_derivation: o splits into ue under stress.

puedes.etymology_derivation: Chains directly with a bare infinitive.

dormir.etymology_derivation: Latin dormīre — English dormitory and dormant.

empezar.english_meaning: to begin, to start (empiezo: I start)
empezar.shift_rule: Boot verb e → ie (takes a before infinitive)
empezar.context_phrase: La clase empieza a las nueve.
empezar.etymology_derivation: Takes a before a following infinitive: empiezo a comprender ('I'm starting to understand').

preferir.etymology_derivation: Stem-changing e → ie in the boot: prefiero, prefieres, prefiere.

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

tener.etymology_derivation: Latin tenēre ('to hold'). While other tongues used 'have' (like French avoir), Spanish promoted 'hold' (tener) to main possession.

tenemos.shift_rule: 1st person plural of tener (outside the boot!)
tenemos.etymology_derivation: Because the stress moves onto the ending (-ne-mos), the stem vowel e stays unchanged!

mostrar.shift_rule: Boot verb o → ue (root of demostrar)
mostrar.context_translation: Will you show me the way?
mostrar.etymology_derivation: Highlighted in Language Transfer: mostrar ('to show') and demostrar ('to demonstrate/prove') share the exact same o → ue boot!

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
